title: The hypertrophy series: the optimal number of sets per muscle group
summary: NH argues the optimal set count is the lowest that keeps strength and tonnage progressing, because set count is limited by muscular endurance and frequency eventually becomes the main lever. He gives a sandbagging test, explains set sacrifice, and links set count to rep ranges through evolving references.
claims: Sets and reps matter equally; volume cannot be separated from intensity or frequency
Use as few sets as possible while progression continues; drop from 15 to 12 sets if you still progress, even if 3 more sets would add a tiny bit
Frequency eventually becomes the main lever for adding tonnage and training time is finite, so be stingy with sets
Bigger muscles have better muscular endurance; adapt set counts to how advanced each body part is
A newly isolated small muscle like the rear delts tolerates only 3-4 meaningful sets per workout; jumping to 12 weekly sets is unrealistic and signals sandbagging
Without relevant intensity windows you need far more sets; fixing intensity cuts sets and speeds progress
Sandbag test: if you do 5 sets, try 7 with the same reps; if you can, the weight is too light, add load
The real cap on sets is muscular endurance, so every set must mean something
Remove sets kept for pump or enjoyment that do nothing for progression (set sacrifice) when you need room or time
Changing set count requires changing weight or reps (evolving references)
Higher rep work fits more sets: a first set of 15 can be followed by 14, 13 and 12 across four sets, better than a single set
A true 3RM cannot be repeated for four sets; high-intensity work needs few sets
